01API Gateway & Service-to-Service Entry
Start with the API Gateway problem, its responsibilities, service discovery, routing, authentication, logging and load balancing.
Interview-ready
Level 2: API Gateway Pattern | Communication Patterns API Gateway ├── Authentication(Each request is stateless, so authentication

needed for all the incoming request)

├── Rate Limiting(How many request sent by client or service) ├── Routing(Routing ensures that incoming requests are forwarded

to the appropriate microservice based on the API path.)

├── Logging └── Load Balancing(Service A has 5 instances, choose one) └── Service Discovery(Gateway won’t know where services are, ask registry like eureka) API Gateway acts as a single entry point in a microservices architecture. It handles

authentication since requests are stateless, applies rate limiting to protect backend services, routes requests to appropriate microservices , logs request details for monitoring and debugging, and performs load balancing across multiple service instances.” --------------------- In a microservices architecture, having multiple services means the client would need to know each service’s endpoint , which increases complexity and tight coupling. To solve this, we introduce an API Gateway that acts as a single entry point. It handles routing requests to appropriate services, and also manages cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and logging.

🧠 1. Problem (Without API Gateway) Client → User Service Client → Payment Service Client → Hotel Service

Client → Rating Service ❌ Issues: Client must know: IP, Port, endpoints If service changes: Client must update ❌ Too many network calls: Poor performance ❌ No centralized: Authentication ❌ Rate limiting ❌ Logging ❌

🧠 2. Solution (API Gateway) Client → API Gateway → Microservices ✅ What Gateway Does: 👉 Acts as single entry point 🔥 Responsibilities: Routing: /user → User Service /payment → Payment Service Authentication: Validate JWT / API Key Rate Limiting: Limit requests per user Load Balancing: Distribute requests across instances Aggregation: Combine multiple service responses
🔹 Service Discovery 👉 Responsible for: - Keeping track of all service instances
- Mapping: service name → IP/port - Example: User Service → 10.0.1.2:8080 Payment Service → 10.0.1.5:8080 1. Client → API Gateway 2. Gateway receives request (/user) 3. Gateway asks Service Discovery: "Where is User Service?" 4. Discovery returns instance list 5. Gateway picks one (load balancing) 6. Request forwarded
🧠 2. Rate Limiting (You are close, but refine it) 🔥 Correct understanding: Rate limiting = control how many requests are ALLOWED per user Example: User can send 10 requests per second ❗ Important: It’s NOT about server capacity It’s about protecting system Better explanation: “Rate limiting ensures that a client does not send too many requests in a given time window,

protecting backend services from overload.”

🧠 3. Authentication (Perfect understanding ✅ ) You said: “Each request is stateless, so authentication needed” 👉 ✅ Correct Why?

HTTP is stateless So every request must include: JWT / API Key / Session Token Interview line: “Since APIs are stateless, authentication must be validated for every request at the gateway.”

🧠 4. Logging (You said you don’t know — let’s fix that 🔥 ) What is Logging? Record every request and response details Why important? Debugging issues Monitoring traffic Auditing (who did what) Example: UserID=123 called /payment at 10:30 → success Interview line: “Logging helps in monitoring, debugging, and auditing system behavior by capturing request

and response details.”

🧠 5. Routing (Correct ✅, let’s sharpen) You said: “Gateway decides which microservice to call” 👉 ✅ Correct Example: /api/user → User Service /api/payment → Payment Service Interview line: “Routing ensures that incoming requests are forwarded to the appropriate microservice based

on the API path.”

🧠 6. Load Balancing (Very Good Understanding 🔥 ) You said: “Service A has 5 instances, choose one” 👉 ✅ PERFECT Example: User Service instances: U1, U2, U3, U4, U5 Gateway will: Request 1 → U1 Request 2 → U2 Request 3 → U3 Why? Distribute load Improve performance Avoid overload Interview line: “Load balancing distributes requests across multiple service instances to ensure high

availability and efficient resource utilization.” Trade-off? What is a Trade-off? A trade-off is a design decision where improving one aspect of the system requires compromising another. There is no perfect architecture. Every design choice has advantages and disadvantages. Senior developers and architects are expected to explain why they chose a particular design based on business requirements. How to Explain a Trade-off in an Interview

02Architectural Trade-offs
Use trade-offs as the core architect reasoning model: requirement → options → decision → benefits → trade-offs → why acceptable.
Use this framework for every architectural decision: Requirement ↓ Possible Options ↓ Chosen Solution ↓ Benefits ↓ Trade-offs ↓ Why the Trade-off is Acceptable Example Requirement The application receives millions of read requests. Possible Options Read directly from the database Use Redis Cache Chosen Solution Redis Cache Benefits Faster response time Reduced database load Trade-offs Users may occasionally receive slightly stale data. Cache invalidation adds complexity. Why Acceptable Product information changes infrequently, so slight staleness is acceptable for significantly

better performance. Common Trade-offs in System Design 1. Performance vs Consistency Goal Improve response time. Solution Use Redis Cache. Benefits Faster API response Reduced database load Better user experience Trade-offs Cached data may become stale. Cache invalidation can be complex. Real-world Examples Amazon product pages News websites E-commerce catalogs Interview Statement Since the application is read-heavy, I would introduce Redis caching to reduce database load and improve response time. The trade-off is that users may occasionally see stale data, which is acceptable because product information doesn't change frequently. 2. Availability vs Consistency (CAP Theorem) Scenario A database node goes down. Option 1 – Prioritize Availability Benefits System remains online. Users can continue using the application. Trade-offs Some users may see outdated data. Option 2 – Prioritize Consistency Benefits Every user sees the latest data. Trade-offs System may temporarily reject requests. Real-world Examples Consistency First Banking Payment systems Availability First Facebook Instagram Twitter Interview Statement For banking applications, consistency is more important than availability because incorrect balances are unacceptable. For social media, availability is preferred since temporary stale data is usually acceptable. 3. Read Performance vs Write Performance Solution Create database indexes. Benefits Faster SELECT queries. Improved search performance. Trade-offs INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations become slower. Additional storage is required. Example CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email); Interview Statement Since users frequently search by email, I would create an index on the email column. This significantly improves read performance for search queries. The trade-off is that INSERT, UPDATE, and

DELETE

operations require maintaining the index, which adds some overhead to write operations.

INSERT │ ├── Write row │ └── Update index (B-Tree/Hash)

4. Scalability vs Cost Solution Horizontal Scaling Benefits Supports millions of users. Easy to add servers. High availability. Trade-offs Increased infrastructure costs. More operational complexity. Interview Statement Instead of using a larger server, I would scale horizontally. While this increases infrastructure costs, it provides better scalability and fault tolerance. 5. Simplicity vs Flexibility Monolithic Architecture Benefits Easy to develop. Easy to test. Easier debugging. Simple deployment. Trade-offs Difficult to scale individual modules. Entire application must be redeployed. Microservices Benefits Independent deployment. Independent scaling. Better fault isolation. Trade-offs Distributed system complexity. Network latency. Service discovery. Monitoring becomes more challenging. Interview Statement For a small startup, I would choose a monolith because it is simpler and faster to develop. As the application grows, microservices become beneficial despite the additional operational complexity. 6. Security vs User Experience Solution Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Benefits Better account protection. Reduced risk of unauthorized access. Trade-offs Additional login step. Slightly reduced user convenience. Real-world Examples Banking applications Government portals Interview Statement For financial systems, stronger security is more important than login convenience. 7. Database Normalization vs Performance Normalized Database Benefits Reduced data duplication. Better consistency. Easier updates. Trade-offs More JOIN operations. Slower read queries. Denormalized Database Benefits Faster reads. Fewer JOIN operations. Trade-offs Data duplication. More difficult updates. Real-world Examples Data warehouses Analytics platforms Reporting systems 8. Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication Synchronous Benefits Immediate response. Easier to understand and debug. Trade-offs Higher latency. Tighter coupling. Dependent services can slow down the request.

Asynchronous (Kafka, RabbitMQ) Benefits Faster API response. Better scalability. Loose coupling. Trade-offs Eventual consistency. More complex debugging and error handling. Example Synchronous Create Order ↓ Send Email ↓ Generate Invoice ↓ Update Inventory ↓ Return Response Asynchronous Create Order ↓ Publish Event ↓ Return 200 OK Background Processing Email Service Inventory Service

Invoice Service Interview Statement I would process non-critical tasks asynchronously to improve user response time while accepting eventual consistency. 9. Storage vs Speed Solution Caching Benefits Faster data access. Reduced database load. Trade-offs Increased memory usage. Cache invalidation complexity. Possible stale data. 10. Strong Consistency vs Eventual Consistency Strong Consistency Benefits Every user sees the latest data immediately. Trade-offs Higher latency. Lower availability during failures. Examples Banking Stock trading Payment processing Eventual Consistency Benefits Better scalability. High availability. Lower latency. Trade-offs Users may temporarily see outdated data. Examples Instagram likes Facebook feeds DNS Amazon product reviews Interview Answer Template Whenever you propose a design, structure your explanation like this: Requirement: The application is read-heavy. Possible Options: Read directly from the database or introduce a cache. Chosen Solution: Use Redis as a caching layer. Benefits: Reduces database load and improves response time. Trade-offs: Cached data may be stale, and cache invalidation adds complexity. Why Acceptable: Product information changes infrequently, so slight staleness is acceptable while achieving much better performance.

Quick Interview Checklist Whenever you make an architectural decision, explain: What is the requirement? What are the possible options? Which solution did you choose? What are its benefits? What are the trade-offs? Why is this trade-off acceptable for this system? Remember: Interviewers are not looking for the "perfect" architecture. They want to see that you can make informed decisions, understand the consequences, and justify your choices based on the system's requirements. System Design github

04API Idempotency & Reliable Retries
Understand idempotency from HTTP semantics through idempotency keys, stored state, retries, concurrency and payment failure reconciliation.
Interview-ready

For operations that naturally produce the same result, explicit idempotency handling may not be necessary.

PUT vs PATCH — Idempotency PUT PUT is idempotent by definition. Suppose we have: PUT /users/101 {"name": "Amit", "email": "amit@example.com" } Send it once: User 101 → name=Amit Send it again: User 101 → name=Amit Send it 10 times: User 101 → name=Amit The final state is the same. ------ Why? Because PUT represents replacement/update of the resource with the provided

representation . The server essentially says: "Make resource 101 look like this." So repeating the same request produces the same final state. PATCH This is where the interview question gets interesting. PATCH is not inherently idempotent. It depends on how the PATCH operation is designed. Idempotent PATCH How do we maintain idempotency? For APIs where duplicate requests are possible, especially payments/order systems, we can use an Idempotency Key .

Example: PATCH /payments/123 Idempotency-Key: abc-123 The server stores: abc-123 → already processed If the same request comes again: PATCH /payments/123 Idempotency-Key: abc-123 The server recognizes the key and doesn't perform the operation again. what to store against the Idempotency-Key and what to return when the same key comes

again .? For operations where duplicate execution is dangerous, such as payments or order creation, I would use an idempotency key. I would store the key together with a request fingerprint and processing state in Redis or a database. When the request succeeds, I would store the final HTTP status and response and return that same response for subsequent retries. For a confirmed business failure, I can also store the failure response. However, for infrastructure failures such as timeouts or 5xx responses, I wouldn't blindly invalidate the key because the downstream operation may already have succeeded. I would keep the request in a processing or unknown state and reconcile the outcome before allowing another execution. 2. Where Do We Need Idempotency? Use idempotency when repeating an operation can create an unwanted business side effect . Common use cases Payment creation Order creation Money transfer Booking/reservation Subscription creation Sending external commands Inventory updates Message processing Creating a customer/account Any API where duplicate execution is dangerous Less important For operations that naturally produce the same result, explicit idempotency handling may not be necessary. 3. HTTP Idempotency vs Idempotency Key These are related but different. HTTP-level idempotency HTTP defines certain methods as idempotent, such as: GET PUT DELETE HEAD OPTIONS The important point is that idempotency is about the intended effect of repeating the request . Idempotency Key For operations such as: POST /payments which may create a new resource, we can use: Idempotency-Key: abc-123 The server uses this key to recognize: "This is the same logical operation that I have already seen."

4. How Do We Determine the Idempotency Key? Best approach Usually the client generates a unique idempotency key for each logical business operation. Example: Payment operation ↓ Idempotency-Key: 8f7a-91ab-.... The same key should be reused when the client retries the same logical operation. Important Do not generate a completely new key for every retry. Wrong: Attempt 1 → key=A Attempt 2 → key=B Attempt 3 → key=C The server sees three different operations. Correct: Attempt 1 → key=A Attempt 2 → key=A Attempt 3 → key=A

5. Should We Generate the Key From the Request Body Hash? A useful distinction: Idempotency Key Idempotency-Key: abc-123 should normally be the primary identity of the logical operation. Request Hash / Fingerprint You can additionally calculate: hash(method + endpoint + relevant request body) and store it alongside the key. Example: Key: abc-123 Request Hash: XYZ789 This allows the server to detect misuse. 6. Same Key + Different Request First request: Idempotency-Key: abc-123 {"amount": 100 } Later: Idempotency-Key: abc-123 {"amount": 500 } This should not be treated as the same operation. The server should reject it, for example: 409 Conflict because the same idempotency key has been associated with a different request.. 7. What Does the Server Store? A typical idempotency record can contain: Idempotency Key Request Hash Status HTTP Status Code Response Body Relevant Response Headers Created At Expiry / TTL For example: Key: abc-123 Request Hash: XYZ789 Status: COMPLETED HTTP Status: 201 Response: {"paymentId": "P1001", "status": "SUCCESS" } TTL: 24 hours Redis is commonly suitable for fast idempotency tracking, while a database may be preferable when the record needs stronger durability or business-level persistence. 22. Idempotency vs Retry Retry Try the request again. Idempotency Make sure the retry doesn't create a duplicate business effect. 23. Idempotency vs Circuit Breaker Retry Attempts again. Circuit Breaker Stops calls when a dependency is repeatedly failing. Idempotency Prevents duplicate business effects. I would require the client to send an idempotency key for each logical payment operation. On the server, I would atomically register that key along with a request fingerprint and a

PROCESSING

state in Redis or a database. If the request completes successfully, I would store the final status and response. If the same key is received again with the same request, I would return the stored response without executing the payment again. If the same key is used with a different request, I would reject it. For payment failures, I would distinguish confirmed failures from unknown outcomes. A timeout or 5xx doesn't necessarily mean the payment failed because the provider may already have processed it. In that case I would keep the operation in an unknown/processing state and reconcile with the payment provider before retrying.

Things to remember: 1. One Idempotency-Key = One logical operation 2. Same key + same request → return existing result 3. Same key + different request → reject 4. Concurrent same key → atomic lock/create → only one request executes 5. Payment timeout → don't assume failure → reconcile before executing again

DNS Vs Load balaner | How to resolve nearest location DNS can be configured with multiple IP addresses for the same hostname. Using GeoDNS or latency-based routing, it returns the IP address of the nearest or healthiest regional load balancer based on the client's location or network latency.

Suppose your domain is: api.example.com and you have four regional load balancers: US Load Balancer → 52.10.10.10 Europe Load Balancer → 18.20.20.20 Asia Load Balancer → 13.30.30.30 Australia Load Balancer → 15.40.40.40
05DNS, Networking & Global Request Routing
Follow how a client resolves a domain, reaches a public entry point, uses load balancing, and reaches CDN or backend infrastructure.
Interview-ready

Step 1: DNS Configuration DNS provider (e.g., Route 53, Cloudflare, Azure DNS) is configured with multiple records for the same hostname.

Conceptually: api.example.com → US LB IP → Europe LB IP → Asia LB IP → Australia LB IP The DNS service knows that these records belong to the same hostname.

Step 2: User Makes a Request A user in Germany opens: https://api.example.com/users The browser asks DNS: What is the IP address of api.example.com? Step 3: Geo DNS Makes the Decision The DNS server sees the request is coming from Germany (based on the resolver's location/IP) and returns:

api.example.com │ ▼ Europe Load Balancer IP 18.20.20.20 A user in Japan asking the same question might get: api.example.com │ ▼ Asia Load Balancer IP 13.30.30.30 So yes, GeoDNS is aware of geographic routing policies.
User (Germany) │ ▼ DNS │ Returns Europe LB │ ▼ Europe Load Balancer │ ▼ API Gateway / Ingress │ ▼ User Service

Architecture questions First, I understand the business problem, expected users, growth expectations, success criteria, and key business outcomes. Based on that, I work with stakeholders to establish architecture principles such as security, availability, and cloud strategy. Then I identify the required functional and technical capabilities, evaluate architecture concerns like performance, scalability, and recoverability, select appropriate patterns such as microservices or event-driven architecture, and finally choose the technology components that best satisfy those requirements and constraints.

💻 Windows ipconfig /displaydns 🧹 Clear: ipconfig /flushdns 🐧 Mac sudo dscacheutil -cachedump -entries Host Clear: sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder Load Balancer | uses private IP for internal services communication

Private IPs are used for internal communication between servers

within a network. In a typical architecture, clients connect to a load balancer using a

public

IP, and the load balancer routes requests to backend servers using their

private

IPs. This improves security by preventing direct access to servers and allows better control over traffic routing. WHAT IS PRIVATE IP? 👉 Think of private IP like an internal room number inside a building 🏢 Analogy Building Address (Public IP) = 88.88.88.1 Room numbers (Private IPs) = 10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2 👉 From outside: You can only reach the building ❗ 👉 Inside building: You can go to specific rooms

🧠 2. PUBLIC IP vs PRIVATE IP 🌐 Public IP - Accessible from internet - Example: 88.88.88.1 - Used by clients (users)

🔒 Private IP - Internal network only - Example: 10.0.0.1 - Used between servers 👉 Key rule: Internet ❌ cannot access private IP directly

🧠 3. YOUR FLOW (STEP-BY-STEP STORY) 🌍 Step 1: User Request User → mywebsite.com
🌐 Step 2: DNS Resolution mywebsite.com → 88.88.88.1 (Public IP) 👉 This IP belongs to: Load Balancer
⚖ Step 3: Load Balancer Receives Request User → Load Balancer (Public IP) 👉 Now decision: Which server should handle this?
🔀 Step 4: Load Balancer Routes Request Load Balancer → Server1 (10.0.0.1) OR → Server2 (10.0.0.2) 👉 These are: Private IPs 🔒
🧠 4. WHY PRIVATE IP? (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) 🔐 1. SECURITY Clients cannot directly hit servers 👉 Without private IP: User → Server directly ❌ (dangerous) 👉 With private IP: User → Load Balancer → Server ✅

⚙ 2. CONTROL Load balancer controls: - Routing - Load distribution - Failover 💰 3. COST & SCALING Private IPs are cheap and unlimited inside network

🧠 5. REAL CLOUD EXAMPLE (IMPORTANT)
AWS Example: Internet → ALB (Public IP) ↓ Private EC2 instances (10.x.x.x) 👉 Same concept in: Azure → VNet GCP → VPC
🧠 6. FINAL MENTAL MODEL (🔥 ) User (Internet) ↓ DNS → Public IP ↓ Load Balancer (Public) ↓ Private Network ↓ Server1 (10.x.x.x) Server2 (10.x.x.x)

🧠 2. Why DNS is Needed Humans: Use domain names (easy) Machines: Use IP addresses 👉 DNS bridges this gap
🧠 3. When DNS is Used 👉 DNS is used: Before every network call (first time) Examples: API call → Gateway CDN call → video/image Website load
🧠 4. DNS Flow (Step-by-Step)

1. Client enters URL 2. DNS lookup happens 3. IP address returned 4. Client connects to that IP

🧠 5. Full DNS Resolution (Advanced but Important) Client → Local Cache ↓ (miss) ISP DNS ↓ (miss) Root Server ↓ TLD Server (.com) ↓ Authoritative DNS ↓ Returns IP
🧠 6. DNS Caching (VERY IMPORTANT) 👉 DNS is NOT called every time Why? To reduce latency TTL (Time To Live) Defines how long DNS result is cached Example: TTL = 5 minutes → no DNS call for 5 minutes
🧠 7. DNS + API Gateway Flow Client → api.netflix.com ↓ DNS resolves to Load Balancer IP ↓ Request → API Gateway
↓ Backend services
🧠 8. DNS + CDN Flow (VERY IMPORTANT) Client → cdn.netflix.com ↓ DNS returns NEAREST CDN server ↓ Client connects to that CDN
🧠 9. Key Insight (🔥 ) 👉 DNS behaves differently: only when DNS has power to decide cdn vs backend For API: Returns Load Balancer IP For CDN: Returns nearest server IP (Geo DNS)
🧠 10. Geo DNS (Advanced 🔥 ) 👉 DNS can route based on: - User location - Latency - Server availability Example: User India → India CDN User US → US CDN
🧠 11. DNS vs API Gateway vs CDN DNS = "Where to go?" Gateway = "What to do?" CDN = "Here is your data"
🧠 12. What DNS DOES NOT DO ❌ Does NOT process request ❌ Does NOT route logic ❌ Does NOT authenticate
👉 Only: Resolve domain → IP
🧠 13. Full System Flow (Combined) Client ├── API Request │ ↓ │ DNS → Load Balancer → Gateway → Backend │ └── CDN Request ↓ DNS → nearest CDN → serve content
🧠 14. Interview-Ready Answer “DNS is responsible for resolving domain names into IP addresses. It enables clients to locate

servers for API Gateway or CDN. In advanced setups like CDN, DNS also performs geo-based routing to direct users to the nearest server.”

🧪 🔥 Q&A (VERY IMPORTANT) ❓ Does DNS decide API vs CDN? 👉 ❌ NO URL decides destination
❓ Is DNS called every time? 👉 ❌ NO Uses caching (TTL)
❓ Who decides nearest CDN server? 👉 ✅ DNS Geo-based routing
❓ Who decides which API Gateway instance? 👉 ❌ DNS 👉 ✅ Load Balancer
DNS → LB → Gateway instance
❓ Is DNS an interceptor? 👉 ❌ NO DNS = lookup system
❓ How many times DNS is used? 👉 Depends: At least once per domain (api + cdn = multiple)
❓ What happens if DNS cache expires? New DNS lookup happens
🧠 15. Real World Tools Google DNS (8.8.8.8) AWS Route 53 Cloudflare DNS
🧠 16. One-Line Summary DNS = maps domain names to IP addresses and helps locate the correct server

Data Partitioning Data Partitioning https://github.com/junfanz1/Software-Engineer-Coding-Interviews/blob/main/Grokking%20the%20System%20Design%20Interview/Grokking%20the%20System%20Design%20Interview.md 14.1. Partitioning Criteria 1. Key or Hash-based partitioning Under this scheme, we apply a hash function to some key attributes of the entity we are storing; that yields the partition number. For example, if we have 100 DB servers and our ID is a numeric value that gets incremented by one each time a new record is inserted. In this example, the hash function could be ‘ID % 100’, which will give us the server number where we can store/read that record. This approach should ensure a uniform allocation of data among servers. The fundamental problem with this approach is that it effectively fixes the total number of DB servers, since adding new servers means changing the hash function which would require redistribution of data and downtime for the service. A workaround for this problem is to use Consistent Hashing. 2. List partitioning In this scheme, each partition is assigned a list of values, so whenever we want to insert a new record, we will see which partition contains our key and then store it there. For example, we can decide all users living in Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, or Denmark will be stored in a

07Data Partitioning & Rebalancing
Understand partitioning strategies and the practical problems of joins, referential integrity and rebalancing.

partition for the Nordic countries. 3. Round-robin partitioning This is a very simple strategy that ensures uniform data distribution. With ‘n’ partitions, the ‘i’ tuple is assigned to partition (i mod n). 4. Composite partitioning Under this scheme, we combine any of the above partitioning schemes to devise a new scheme. For example, first applying a list partitioning scheme and then a hash based partitioning. Consistent hashing could be considered a composite of hash and list partitioning where the hash reduces the key space to a size that can be listed. 14.2. Common Problems of Data Partitioning Joins and Denormalization Performing joins on a database which is running on one server is straightforward, but once a database is partitioned and spread across multiple machines it is often not feasible to perform joins that span database partitions. Such joins will not be performance efficient since data has to be compiled from multiple servers. A common workaround for this problem is to denormalize the database so that queries that previously required joins can be performed from a single table. Of course, the service now has to deal with all the perils of denormalization such as data inconsistency. Referential integrity As we saw that performing a cross-partition query on a partitioned database is not feasible, similarly, trying to enforce data integrity constraints such as foreign keys in a partitioned database can be extremely difficult. Most of RDBMS do not support foreign keys constraints across databases on different database servers. Which means that applications that require referential integrity on partitioned databases often have to enforce it in application code. Often in such cases, applications have to run regular SQL jobs to clean up dangling references. Rebalancing There could be many reasons we have to change our partitioning scheme: The data distribution is not uniform, e.g., there are a lot of places for a particular ZIP code that cannot fit into one database partition. There is a lot of load on a partition, e.g., there are too many requests being handled by the DB partition dedicated to user photos. In such cases, either we have to create more DB partitions or have to rebalance existing partitions, which means the partitioning scheme changed and all existing data moved to new locations. Doing this without incurring downtime is extremely difficult. Using a scheme like directory based partitioning does make rebalancing a more palatable experience at the cost of increasing the complexity of the system and creating a new single point of failure (i.e. the lookup service/database). 1. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation 🧠 What is Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation? 👉 Quick calculations to estimate scale, capacity, and performance WITHOUT exact numbers. 📌 Think: “Rough idea is enough — not exact precision” Memory: estimates

1 KB = 10^3 1 MB = 10^6 1 GB = 10^9 1 TB = 10^12 1 PB =10^15
🧠 Cheat Sheet (Memorize This)
1 KB = 10^3 1 MB = 10^6 1 GB = 10^9 1 TB = 10^12 1 day = 86400 seconds RPS(Request per second) = Total Requests / 86400
💡 Real-Life Analogy Before building a system, you ask: How many users? How much data? How many requests per second? 👉 Like planning: “How many chairs do I need for a wedding?”
1 ⃣ Power of 2 (Memory Basics) This is SUPER important because computers use binary (base 2) 🧠 Trick to remember: 👉 Every +10 power ≈ ×1000
2 ⃣ Latency Numbers (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) These are “ numbers every programmer should know ” Operation - Time CPU cache -~1 ns RAM ~100 ns SSD ~100 µs Network ~100 ms 🧠 Insight: 👉 Network is 1 million times slower than memory
3 ⃣ Availability (Uptime %) Availability Downtime/year 99% ~3.65 days 99.9% ~8.7 hours 99.99% ~52 min 99.999% ~5 min 🧠 Interview Tip: “5 nines = highly reliable system”
🧮 How to Actually Do BOE (Step-by-Step) Let’s take a real interview example 👇
🎯 Example: Design Instagram Step 1: Users Assume: 100M users Step 2: Daily Active Users (DAU) 10% active → 10M users/day Step 3: Requests per second (RPS) Assume: Each user → 10 requests/day 👉 Total requests/day: 10M × 10 = 100M requests/day 👉 Convert to seconds: 100M / 86400 ≈ 1157 requests/sec (~1K RPS) Step 4: Storage Estimation Assume: 1 photo = 1 MB = 10^6 bytes 2M uploads/day, 2M = 2 × 10^6 photos
👉 Storage/day: 2M × 1MB = 2TB/day 👉 Storage/year: 2TB × 365 ≈ 730TB/year
🔍 Step-by-Step Breakdown Step 1 ⃣ What is 2M? 👉 2M uploads/day = 2 million photos/day So: 2M = 2 × 10^6 photos

Step 2 ⃣ Size of each photo 1 photo = 1 MB = 10^6 bytes Step 3 ⃣ Multiply both Now total storage per day: Total = (number of photos) × (size per photo) So: = (2 × 10^6) × (10^6) Step 4 ⃣ Multiply powers 👉 Rule: 10^a × 10^b = 10^(a+b) So: = 2 × 10^(6+6) = 2 × 10^12 bytes

💡 Now convert to TB We know: 1 TB ≈ 10^12 bytes So: 2 × 10^12 bytes ≈ 2 TB =============================================

10Case Study — Social Media / News Feed
A complete social/news feed design centered on feed publishing and retrieval, including fanout choices and caching.
Case study mode: learn the requirements, architecture, flow, scaling decisions, components, trade-offs and interview closing as one connected story.
Interview-readyUse casesArchitecture flowTrade-offs

Design A News Feed System | Facebook | Twitter “A news feed system is designed around two core flows: feed publishing and feed retrieval. When a user creates a post, it is stored in the database and pushed to friends’ feeds using a fanout service. To handle scalability, a hybrid fanout model is used where most users follow a push model, while high-follower users use a pull model. The news feed itself is stored in cache as a list of post IDs for fast retrieval. When a user opens the app, the system fetches these IDs, retrieves full post and user details from cache, and serves media via CDN. Message queues are used to decouple fanout processing, and graph databases are used to manage user relationships.” Feed cache is user-specific and stores a list of post IDs representing that user’s timeline. Post cache, on the other hand, is a shared global cache that stores the actual content of posts. This separation ensures memory efficiency and allows fast feed retrieval without duplicating post data. “Fanout is based on the number of followers, not the type of user receiving the content. So if a celebrity follows a normal user, they will receive posts via push. However, for celebrities posting to millions of followers, the system avoids pushing updates and instead uses a pull-based approach.” “When a celebrity publishes a post, it is stored in the post database and cache, but not pushed to followers’ feed caches. Instead, when a user retrieves their feed, the system dynamically fetches posts from celebrities they follow and merges them with the precomputed feed.” 🎬 🧠 NEWS FEED SYSTEM — COMPLETE STORY (FINAL) 🎯 1. INTRO (HOW YOU START) “Let’s design a news feed system like Facebook or Instagram where users can post content and see posts from people they follow in real time.” “The system needs to support millions of users, provide low latency feed loading, and handle high fanout scenarios like celebrities.” 🧩 2. CORE REQUIREMENTS Functional: - User can create post - User can see feed (timeline) - Feed sorted by latest / ranked

Non-Functional: - Low latency (fast feed loading) - High scalability (millions of users) - High availability
🏗 3. CORE IDEA (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) 👉 Entire system revolves around 2 flows: 1. Feed Publishing (Write path) 2. Feed Retrieval (Read path)

✍ 4. FLOW 1 — FEED PUBLISHING (WRITE) 🎬 Scenario: User A posts Step 1: Store Post User A → Post Service 👉 Stored in: Post DB Post Cache (GLOBAL) 👉 Example: post:101 → "Hello world" Step 2: Fanout Decision (CRITICAL 🔥 ) 👉 System checks: Is user normal OR celebrity? 🟢 CASE 1 — NORMAL USER (Fanout-on-Write) Example: User A has 100 followers

Step: Push post to all followers 👉 Feed cache updated: feed:UserB → [post101, post99, post88] 👉 Important: Only post_id stored

🔴 CASE 2 — CELEBRITY (Fanout-on-Read) Example: Celebrity has 10M followers 👉 Instead of push: NO fanout ❌ 👉 Only: Store post in Post Cache

🧠 5. WHY DIFFERENT APPROACH? Normal user: Few followers → push is cheap
Celebrity: Millions followers → push is expensive ❌ 👉 Solution: Hybrid Model 🔥

📖 6. FLOW 2 — FEED RETRIEVAL (READ) 🎬 Scenario: User B opens app Step 1: Get normal feed Fetch from Feed Cache 👉 Example: [p10, p20, p30] Step 2: Get celebrity posts Fetch from Post Cache / DB 👉 Query: “Give latest posts from celebrities B follows” Step 3: Merge feeds (IMPORTANT 🔥 ) Final Feed = Normal posts (cache) + Celebrity posts (dynamic)

Step 4: Hydration 👉 Convert IDs → full content post_id → Post Cache → full data
🧠 7. CACHE DESIGN (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) 🟢 Feed Cache (User-specific) Key: user_id Value: [post_ids] 👉 Example: feed:1001 → [p1, p2, p3]
🔵 Post Cache (Global) Key: post_id Value: full post content 👉 Example: post:101 → {content, user, media}
🧠 8. FINAL ARCHITECTURE (MENTAL MODEL) User ↓ API Gateway ↓ Post Service ↓ ├── Post Cache (global) ├── Feed Cache (per user) └── DB Feed Retrieval: Feed Cache + Post Cache → Merge → Response
🧠 9. COMPLETE FLOW (FINAL 🔥 ) 📨 When posting User A posts ↓ Store in Post Cache ↓ IF normal user: Push to followers feed cache IF celebrity: NO push
📖 When reading User B opens feed ↓ Get normal feed (cache) ↓ Get celebrity posts (dynamic) ↓ Merge + hydrate
↓ Return feed
🧠 10. KEY INSIGHTS (INTERVIEW GOLD 🔥 ) 🔹 Separation Write path ≠ Read path
🔹 Hybrid model Push + Pull
🔹 Cache optimization Feed → IDs only Post → full data
🔹 Scalability Avoid heavy writes for celebrities
🧠 11. IMPORTANT QUESTIONS & ANSWERS 🔥 ❓ Q1: Why not push celebrity posts? 👉 Too many followers → system overload
❓ Q2: Where are celebrity posts stored? 👉 Post Cache only (global)
❓ Q3: Does celebrity have feed cache? 👉 Yes, for posts from others (normal users)
❓ Q4: Does normal user post go to celebrity? 👉 YES (if celebrity follows them)
❓ Q5: What is stored in feed cache? 👉 Only post_ids
❓ Q6: What is fanout-on-read? 👉 Fetch posts during feed read (pull model)
❓ Q7: What is fanout-on-write? 👉 Push posts to followers (push model)
❓ Q8: Why separate post cache and feed cache? 👉 Avoid duplication Save memory Improve performance
❓ Q9: How is final feed generated? 👉 Feed Cache + Celebrity Posts → Merge
❓ Q10: Biggest challenge? 👉 Fanout scaling (celebrity problem)

How to check DNS cache in browser? “Browsers maintain a DNS cache to store domain-to-IP mappings for faster access. In Chrome, this can be viewed using chrome://net-internals/#dns, where cached entries can also be cleared.” 1. chrome://net-internals/#dns

11Case Study — E-commerce
A full e-commerce architecture with functional/non-functional requirements, data stores, search, recommendations, orders, scaling and asynchronous processing.
Case study mode: learn the requirements, architecture, flow, scaling decisions, components, trade-offs and interview closing as one connected story.
Interview-readyUse casesArchitecture flowTrade-offs

Amazon This e-commerce system is designed using a microservices architecture where different services like search, cart, order, and recommendation are independently scalable. Search functionality is handled using ElasticSearch for fast querying. while cart and recommendations use caching to improve performance. The order service ensures strong consistency and interacts with inventory before persisting data in the database. Messaging queues are used for asynchronous processing such as updating recommendations and search indexes. The system uses both SQL and NoSQL databases depending on the use case, and archival strategies are used to keep operational databases efficient. Overall, the system uses microservices architecture with a mix of SQL and NoSQL databases. Search is optimized using Elasticsearch, recommendations are generated using batch processing, and caching is used to reduce latency. Message queues help decouple services, and archival strategies ensure scalability. ============ 🎬 🛒 AMAZON SYSTEM DESIGN — STORY EXPLANATION 🧠 🎯 1. INTRO (HOW YOU START) “Let’s design an e-commerce platform like Amazon. This design will also apply to systems like Flipkart, Walmart, or eBay.”

👉 Then set expectations: “I’ll start with functional requirements, then non-functional requirements, followed by

capacity estimation, database design, APIs, and finally the system architecture with scaling.”

🔥 This opening already gives interviewer confidence.
🧠 🧩 2. FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS (STORY) “Since we have limited time in an interview, we’ll focus only on the core features instead

of everything.”

Core features: “First, users should be able to search for products.” 👉 Story: User opens Amazon → types “iPhone” → expects results instantly. “Second, when users open the homepage, they should see personalized recommendations.” 👉 Story: User opens app → sees “Recommended for you” → based on past behavior. “Third, users should be able to add items to cart and place orders.” 👉 Story: Search → Add to cart → Checkout → Place order. “Fourth, users should be able to check order status.” 👉 Story: User checks: “Is my order shipped?” “Fifth, users should be able to read and write reviews.” 👉 Story: User reads reviews before buying → trust system. Assumptions (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) “To keep scope manageable, I’ll assume user authentication, product onboarding, and payment

systems already exist.”

👉 💡 Interview Tip: This shows: You know how to control scope
🧠 ⚡ 3. NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS (STORY) “Now let’s talk about system behavior expectations.” 🔹 Low Latency “When a user searches or opens homepage, results must appear instantly.” 👉 Story: User won’t wait → system must respond in milliseconds. 🔹 High Consistency “When placing orders or checking order status, data must be accurate.” 👉 Story: User buys 1 item → inventory must not go negative. 👉 💡 Key Insight: Search = speed Order = correctness
🧠 📊 4. CAPACITY ESTIMATION (STORY) “Let’s estimate the scale of the system.” Users: “Assume 300 million monthly users.” Search Traffic: “Each user does ~10 searches per month.” 👉 So: Total = 3 Billion searches/month ≈ 1000 searches/sec 👉 Story:

System must handle 1000 queries every second continuously Storage: “Assume 10 million products, each ~10MB.” 👉 Total: 100 TB storage 👉 Insight: “Most storage is consumed by images and descriptions.”

🧠 🗄 5. DATABASE DESIGN (STORY) 👤 User & Address (SQL) “User data is structured, so we use SQL.” 👉 Story: User has: Name Email Password Multiple addresses 👉 Why separate address? “To avoid duplication and allow multiple addresses.”
📦 Product DB (NoSQL 🔥 ) “Product schema varies a lot, so SQL is inefficient.” 👉 Story: Laptop vs Shoes → completely different fields. 👉 Solution: Use NoSQL (MongoDB / DynamoDB)
🛒 Order DB (NoSQL) “An order can contain multiple items, so storing it as a single document is easier.” 👉 Story: 1 order → 10 items → stored together.
⭐ Review DB (Key-Value) “Reviews are fetched per product, so key-value DB works well.” 👉 Story: Product ID → All reviews
🧠 🔌 6. APIs (STORY) “Now let’s define APIs to interact with system.” Search /search?q=phone Recommendation /recommendations?userId=1 Add to Cart /cart Place Order /order Order Status /order/{id} 👉 Story: Each user action = API call
🧠 🏗 7. HIGH LEVEL DESIGN (MAIN STORY 🔥 )
🔍 Search Flow “User searches → Search Service queries product DB” 👉 Then: “Search data is stored in search history DB” 👉 Why? “To generate recommendations later”
🎯 Recommendation Flow “Batch jobs process search history using ML algorithms” 👉 Story: System learns: User likes phones → show more phones
🛒 Cart Flow “User adds items → stored in cart DB”
📦 Order Flow (CRITICAL 🔥 ) “User places order → system checks inventory → stores order” 👉 Story: User buys iPhone → system checks stock → confirms → creates order.

📊 Order Status “Order status service fetches order from DB”

⭐ Review Flow “User reads/writes reviews via review service”
🧠 🚀 8. SCALING (ADVANCED STORY 🔥 ) 🔹 Load Balancer “Distributes traffic across servers”
🔹 Multiple Instances “Each service runs multiple instances for fault tolerance”
🔹 Elasticsearch “Used for fast search instead of DB queries”
🔹 Database Scaling Master-Slave: Writes → Master Reads → Slaves 👉 Story: Search = read heavy → optimized
🔹 Archival “Old data is moved to archive DB” 👉 Story: Old orders → rarely accessed → keep main DB fast
🔹 Caching (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) “Cache is used for recommendations, reviews, and order status” 👉 Story: User opens app → instant response
🔹 Message Queue
“Used to decouple services and process asynchronously” 👉 Story: Order placed → update recommendations later
🧠 🎯 FINAL INTERVIEW CLOSING “Overall, the system uses microservices architecture with a mix of SQL and NoSQL

databases. Search is optimized using Elasticsearch, recommendations are generated using batch processing, and caching is used to reduce latency. Message queues help decouple services, and archival strategies ensure scalability.”

🧠 2. BEST NEXT SYSTEMS TO STUDY (ORDERED 🔥 ) 🛒 1. E-COMMERCE SYSTEM (HIGH PRIORITY) 👉 Example: Amazon / Flipkart You will learn: - Inventory management - Order flow - Payment system - Distributed transactions 👉 This connects to your Hybris role 🔥
🔍 2. SEARCH SYSTEM (Google / ElasticSearch) Learn: - Indexing - Ranking - Query optimization

12Case Study — Real-Time Chat / WhatsApp
A real-time chat architecture using persistent connections, Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, message storage and supporting APIs.
Case study mode: learn the requirements, architecture, flow, scaling decisions, components, trade-offs and interview closing as one connected story.
Interview-readyUse casesArchitecture flowTrade-offs

REal time chat/ Wahtsapp In a real-time chat system, users connect to WebSocket-based chat servers that maintain persistent connections. When a user sends a message, it is first processed by the connected server and then published to Redis Pub/Sub, which broadcasts the message to all chat servers. Each server checks if the recipient is connected to it, and the appropriate server delivers the message instantly. In parallel, the message is sent to Kafka for asynchronous processing such as storing chat history and analytics. A NoSQL database is typically used for storing messages due to its scalability and high write throughput. This architecture ensures low latency for real-time delivery while maintaining scalability and reliability.” Overall, the system separates real-time communication, message distribution, and asynchronous processing, ensuring low latency for chat while maintaining scalability and reliability. When a user sends a message, it first reaches the WebSocket server, which publishes it to Redis Pub/Sub for real-time delivery. The server holding the recipient delivers the message instantly. In parallel, the message is sent to Kafka for asynchronous processing like storage and analytics. The recipient does not read from Kafka; Kafka is only used for backend processing.

Client (User A / User B) ↓ Load Balancer / API Gateway ↓ WebSocket Chat Servers (multiple) ↓ ├── Redis Pub/Sub (Real-time delivery) ├── Kafka (Async processing) └── Database (Storage) WebSocket Server = Server that communicates using WebSocket protocol HTTP Server → uses HTTP protocol WebSocket Server → uses WebSocket protocol User A ↓ WebSocket Server 1 ↓ ├── Redis → broadcast │ ↓ │ Server 2 → User B │ └── Kafka → async storage Redis = "who should get message now" Kafka = "what to do with message later"
🧠 1. Your Statement (Refined) You said: “WebSocket is a protocol, and WhatsApp connects to a WebSocket server” 👉 ✅ Correct
🧠 2. What is a WebSocket Server? 👉 You asked: “Are we calling it WebSocket server because we used WebSocket protocol?” 👉 ✅ YES — exactly
🧠 3. What Happens Internally Step 1: Connection Establishment Client → HTTP request → Upgrade to WebSocket 👉 After upgrade: Persistent connection established

Step 2: Communication Client ↔ Server (bi-directional) 👉 No repeated requests like HTTP

🧠 4. Why We Call It “WebSocket Server” 👉 Because: It handles: - WebSocket handshake - Persistent connections - Real-time messaging 👉 Not just normal HTTP handling
🔥 Definition WebSocket Server = Server that communicates using WebSocket protocol
DETAILED HLD (CHAT SYSTEM) 🌳 🔥 HIGH LEVEL ARCHITECTURE Client (Mobile/Web) ↓ API Gateway / Load Balancer ↓ WebSocket Chat Servers ↓ Redis Pub/Sub (Message Distribution) ↓ Kafka (Async Processing) ↓ Message Storage + Analytics
🧠 1. REQUIREMENTS Functional: - Send/receive messages in real time - Group chat / channels - Message history - Read receipts
Non-functional: - Low latency (instant delivery) - High scalability (millions users) - High availability
🧠 2. CORE COMPONENTS (DEEP EXPLANATION) 📱 2.1 CLIENT (Mobile/Web) Responsibilities: - Send messages

- Maintain WebSocket connection - Receive messages instantly 👉 Key concept: Persistent connection required 🚪 2.2 API GATEWAY / LOAD BALANCER Responsibilities: - Entry point - Authentication - Route to correct chat server - Load balancing 👉 Same concept as Netflix Gateway

💬 2.3 WEBSOCKET CHAT SERVER (CORE 🔥 ) Why WebSocket? HTTP(stateless) → request-response ❌ WebSocket → persistent connection ✅ Responsibilities: - Maintain connection with users - Send/receive messages instantly Flow: Client ↔ Chat Server (bi-directional) 👉 🔥 MOST IMPORTANT COMPONENT
⚡ 2.4 REDIS PUB/SUB (SCALING 🔥 ) Problem: User A → Server 1 User B → Server 2
Solution: Server 1 → Redis → Server 2 Role: Broadcast messages across servers 👉 Redis = message router

🧵 2.5 KAFKA / MESSAGE QUEUE Why needed? Do NOT block chat flow Responsibilities: - Store messages - Analytics - Notifications - Retry if failure 👉 Flow: Chat Server → Kafka → Consumers 👉 Kafka = async backbone

🗄 2.6 MESSAGE STORAGE Stores: - Chat history - Messages 👉 Accessed via: REST APIs

📊 2.7 ANALYTICS / READ RECEIPTS Examples: - Delivered - Seen - Typing indicators 👉 Processed via Kafka

🧠 3. END-TO-END FLOW (VERY IMPORTANT 🔥 ) 📨 Sending Message 1. Client → WebSocket → Chat Server 2. Chat Server → Redis Pub/Sub 3. Redis → All Chat Servers 4. Chat Server → Deliver to receiver 5. Chat Server → Kafka (async) 6. Kafka → Storage + Analytics
🧠 4. KEY DESIGN DECISIONS (INTERVIEW GOLD) Why WebSocket? Real-time communication Why Redis? Scale across servers Why Kafka? Async processing + reliability Why REST? Fetch history (non real-time) ==================================== ==================================
🧠 🎯 1. WHAT THIS SYSTEM DOES 👉 This architecture handles: Real-time chat (live messages) Scalable message delivery

Async processing (analytics, storage)

🧠 2. HIGH LEVEL FLOW (BIG PICTURE) Client → Gateway → Chat Server → Redis → Kafka → APIs
🧠 3. COMPONENT-BY-COMPONENT EXPLANATION 📱 1. CLIENT (Mobile/Web) 👉 Users: Send messages Receive messages Key Requirement: Low latency (real-time delivery)

🚪 2. API GATEWAY / LOAD BALANCER Role: Entry point for all requests Responsibilities: - Route requests - Load balancing - Authentication 👉 Think: Same as Netflix Gateway

💬 3. REAL-TIME CHAT SERVER (WebSocket) 🔥 👉 This is the MOST IMPORTANT component Why WebSocket? HTTP → request/response ❌ WebSocket → persistent connection ✅

What it does: - Maintains connection with clients - Sends/receives messages instantly Flow: Client ↔ WebSocket Server (bi-directional) 👉 🔥 Interview line: “WebSocket is used for real-time bidirectional communication.”

⚡ 4. REDIS PUB/SUB (CHANNEL MANAGEMENT) 👉 This is used for: Message distribution across servers Problem it solves: 👉 If multiple chat servers: User A connected to Server 1 User B connected to Server 2 Solution: Server 1 → Redis Pub/Sub → Server 2 👉 Redis acts as: Message broadcaster
📡 5. MESSAGE REST API 👉 Used for: - Store messages - Fetch history 👉 Why not WebSocket? WebSocket = real-time REST = persistence + retrieval

🧵 6. KAFKA / MESSAGE QUEUE

👉 Used for: Async processing Examples: - Store messages - Analytics - Notifications 👉 Flow: Chat Server → Kafka → Consumers 👉 🔥 Important: Decouples system

📊 7. ANALYTICS / READ RECEIPTS 👉 Uses Kafka events: - Seen message - Delivered status - Metrics

🧠 4. COMPLETE FLOW (VERY IMPORTANT) 📨 When User Sends Message 1. Client → WebSocket → Chat Server 2. Chat Server → Redis Pub/Sub 3. Redis → All Chat Servers 4. Chat Server → Deliver to receivers 5. Chat Server → Kafka (async) 6. Kafka → Storage / Analytics
🧠 5. WHY EACH COMPONENT EXISTS (INTERVIEW GOLD 🔥 ) Why WebSocket? Real-time bidirectional communication

Why Redis Pub/Sub? Scale across multiple servers Why Kafka? Async processing + reliability Why REST API? Persistence + history retrieval

🧠 6. DESIGN INSIGHTS (VERY IMPORTANT) 🔹 Separation of concerns Real-time → WebSocket Storage → REST Async → Kafka 🔹 Scalability Horizontal scaling of chat servers 🔹 Fault tolerance Kafka ensures message durability
🧠 7. INTERVIEW ANSWER (FINAL 🔥 ) “This architecture supports real-time chat using WebSocket servers that maintain

persistent connections with clients. Messages are distributed across multiple servers using Redis Pub/Sub to ensure scalability. For persistence and history retrieval, REST APIs are used. Kafka is used for asynchronous processing like storing messages and analytics. This separation ensures low latency for real-time communication while maintaining scalability and reliability. ======================= 🎬 🔥 FINAL ANSWER (WHAT YOU SAY) “Let’s say we are designing a real-time chat system like WhatsApp or YouTube live chat, where users can send and receive messages instantly.” “The system is designed for low latency, high availability, and scalability to support millions of concurrent users.” 🚪 Entry “Client requests first go through an API Gateway or load balancer, which handles authentication and routes the request to a chat server.” 💬 Core “For real-time communication, we use WebSocket servers that maintain persistent connections with clients, allowing bi-directional communication.”

⚡ Scaling “Since multiple chat servers are involved, we use Redis Pub/Sub to distribute messages

across servers. This ensures that users connected to different servers can still receive messages.” 🧵 Async “To avoid blocking the chat flow, messages are sent to a message queue like Kafka for asynchronous processing such as storing messages, analytics, and notifications.”

💾 Storage “Message history is stored in a database and can be retrieved using REST APIs when

needed.”

🔥 FINAL CLOSING LINE “Overall, the system separates real-time communication, message distribution, and

asynchronous processing, ensuring low latency for chat while maintaining scalability and reliability.” ==============

🧠 2. FULL MESSAGE FLOW (STEP-BY-STEP 🔥 ) 📨 Scenario: User A sends message to User B 🔹 Step 1: Message Sent User A → WebSocket → Chat Server 1
🔹 Step 2: Server Processes Message Server creates event: {sender: A, receiver: B, message: "Hello", timestamp: T }
🔹 Step 3: Real-Time Path (Redis) Chat Server 1 → Redis Pub/Sub
🔹 Step 4: Redis Broadcast Redis → All Chat Servers
🔹 Step 5: Server Filtering (IMPORTANT 🔥 ) Each server checks: “Is User B connected to me?” Example: Server 1 → No → ignore Server 2 → YES → send to B Server 3 → No → ignore
🔹 Step 6: Delivery Chat Server 2 → User B (WebSocket)

13Case Study — YouTube Live Streaming
A live-video architecture covering ingestion, processing, encoding, segmentation, streaming, CDN, storage and supporting real-time systems.
Case study mode: learn the requirements, architecture, flow, scaling decisions, components, trade-offs and interview closing as one connected story.
Interview-readyUse casesArchitecture flowTrade-offs

Youtube live architecture 🧠 PART 1 — YOUTUBE LIVE HLD (HIGH LEVEL DESIGN) Real-Time Messaging Protocol (RTMP) is a TCP-based technology developed by Macromedia (now Adobe) designed for high-performance, low-latency transmission of audio, video, and data between an encoder and a streaming server. Primarily used for "ingest" in modern live streaming, it sends content from software like OBS to platforms like YouTube or Twitch. “Real-time protocols like RTMP are used in the ingestion phase, where the creator streams video to the platform. After ingestion, the video is processed and converted into HTTP-based streaming protocols like HLS or DASH for scalable distribution to viewers via CDN.

1. Creator → RTMP → Ingestion Server 2. Server → Encode + Segment 3. Convert → HLS/DASH format 4. CDN distributes chunks 5. Client → HTTP → downloads chunks

🌳 🔥 SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (BIG PICTURE) Overall, the system separates ingestion, processing, and delivery, using CDN for scalable distribution and chunk-based streaming for low-latency playback.” “Unlike on-demand systems like Netflix, live streaming introduces additional challenges like low latency and continuous data ingestion. YouTube Live system is focused on live video streaming, real-time playback, real-time interactions like chat and likes, and also supports replay functionality. From a non-functional perspective, the system needs to ensure low latency, high availability, and scalability to support millions of concurrent viewers

Creator → Ingestion ↓ Processing (encode + segment) ↓ Streaming Server ↓ CDN ↓ Client (chunks playback)
🧠 Step 2: Introduce Layers (You started — now refine) You said: “I will explain ingestion which contains entry point operations, processing layer focussed on

encoding and segmentation , streaming or distribution layer, and user layer”

Streaming / Distribution Layer(send chunks to all CDN) 4. Client (Viewer Layer) 5. Supporting Systems (Chat, Storage) 🎥 1. INGESTION LAYER “The ingestion layer acts as the entry point for live streams. The creator uses tools like OBS to

send video streams to the system using protocols like RTMP.”

Internally: Camera → Encoder → RTMP → Ingestion Server Responsibilities: - Accept live stream - Validate stream - Forward to processing layer 👉 🔥 Interview hint: “This is similar to an API Gateway but for video streams.” ⚙ 2. PROCESSING LAYER (CORE LOGIC) “Once the stream is received, it is processed in the processing layer.” 🔹 Encoding / Transcoding Convert into multiple qualities (1080p, 720p, etc.) 🔹 Segmentation (VERY IMPORTANT) “The video is split into small chunks of a few seconds each.”

chunk1.ts chunk2.ts 👉 Say this line: “Segmentation enables continuous streaming instead of downloading the entire video.” 📡 3. STREAMING / DISTRIBUTION LAYER “After processing, the video chunks are sent to streaming servers, which distribute them to CDN edge locations.” Processing(layer 2) → Streaming Server(layer 3) → CDN 🌐 4. CDN (SCALING LAYER 🔥 ) “CDN is responsible for caching and serving video chunks to users from the nearest location.” Why needed: - Reduce latency - Handle large traffic - Improve user experience 👉 🔥 Strong line: “CDN ensures global scalability by serving content from edge servers.” 📱 5. CLIENT / VIEWER LAYER “When a user opens a live stream, the client fetches a manifest file and starts downloading video chunks continuously.”

Flow: Client → CDN → chunk download → playback Player: - Decode chunks - Play video - Adjust quality dynamically 👉 Add: “Adaptive streaming adjusts video quality based on network conditions.”
💾 6. STORAGE (REPLAY) “The live stream is also stored for replay functionality.” ⚡ 7. SUPPORTING SYSTEMS (IMPORTANT) “Real-time chat and likes are handled separately using asynchronous systems.” User actions → Kafka / Pub-Sub → processing 👉 Important: Not used for video streaming ❌ ========================================= Creator (Streamer) ↓RTMP Protocol Ingestion Layer ↓ Processing Layer (Encoding + Segmentation) ↓ Streaming Servers ↓ CDN (Global Distribution) ↓ Viewers (Clients)
🧠 1. REQUIREMENTS Functional: - Live video streaming - Real-time playback - Chat / likes - Replay video
Non-Functional: - Low latency (few seconds) - High availability - Scalability (millions of viewers)
🧠 2. CORE COMPONENTS 🎥 2.1 INGESTION LAYER (ENTRY POINT) 👉 Receives stream from creator OBS / Camera → RTMP → Ingestion Server Responsibilities: - Accept live stream - Validate stream - Forward to processing
⚙ 2.2 PROCESSING LAYER 🔹 Encoding / Transcoding Convert raw video → multiple qualities Example: 1080p, 720p, 480p
🔹 Segmentation (VERY IMPORTANT) Split video → small chunks (2–5 sec) 👉 Output: chunk1.ts chunk2.ts
📡 2.3 STREAMING SERVERS 👉 Intermediate layer: Processing → Streaming Server → CDN Responsibilities: - Push chunks to CDN - Manage live stream session

🌐 2.4 CDN (CORE SCALING LAYER 🔥 )

👉 Most important component Stores + distributes video chunks Responsibilities: - Cache video chunks - Serve nearest users - Handle millions of requests
📱 2.5 CLIENT (VIEWER SIDE) 👉 Viewer opens live video: Client → CDN → Video chunks Player responsibilities: - Fetch chunks continuously - Decode video - Adjust quality (adaptive streaming)
💾 2.6 STORAGE (OPTIONAL) Live stream → stored → replay later
⚡ 2.7 ASYNC SYSTEMS 👉 For non-video tasks: - Chat - Likes - Analytics 👉 Uses: Kafka / Pub-Sub
🧠 3. FULL DATA FLOW (VERY IMPORTANT) Creator → Ingest Server
↓ Encoding + Segmentation ↓ Streaming Server ↓ CDN ↓ Client (chunks playback)
🧠 4. KEY DESIGN DECISIONS (🔥 ) Why segmentation? Continuous streaming instead of full download Why CDN? Global scalability + low latency Why multiple resolutions? Support different network speeds ===========================

INTERVIEW ANSWER (STORY STYLE) 🎬 🔥 FINAL ANSWER (SAY THIS) “Let’s say a creator starts a live stream on YouTube and users start watching it.” (👉 Start with scenario) “The video is first captured and sent to YouTube’s ingestion servers using protocols like RTMP.” (👉 Mention protocol = strong signal) “Once received, the system encodes and transcodes the video into multiple resolutions like 1080p, 720p, etc., to support adaptive streaming.” “The video is then split into small chunks of a few seconds each, which enables continuous streaming rather than downloading the entire video.” (👉 MUST mention segmentation) “These chunks are forwarded to streaming servers, which distribute them to CDN edge locations across the globe.” “When a user opens the live stream, the client fetches a manifest file and starts downloading video chunks from the nearest CDN server.” (👉 CDN + manifest = strong understanding) “The video player continuously decodes and plays these chunks, dynamically adjusting quality based on network conditions.” “Meanwhile, interactions like chat and likes are handled asynchronously using messaging systems, ensuring the main streaming pipeline remains efficient.”

🔥 FINAL CLOSING LINE “Overall, the system separates ingestion, processing, and delivery, using CDN for

scalable distribution and chunk-based streaming for low-latency playback.”

🧠 BONUS (ADD IF YOU WANT TO IMPRESS) “Unlike on-demand systems like Netflix, live streaming introduces additional challenges

like low latency and continuous data ingestion.” ==================================================

👉 What enables adaptive streaming? Multiple resolutions + chunk-based delivery ===================

14Case Study — Netflix
A Netflix-style architecture connecting API control-plane operations with caching, databases, service discovery, recommendations and CDN delivery.
Case study mode: learn the requirements, architecture, flow, scaling decisions, components, trade-offs and interview closing as one connected story.
Interview-readyUse casesArchitecture flowTrade-offs

Netflix Architecture Netflix uses a microservices-based architecture where client requests go through an API Gateway that handles routing, authentication, and rate limiting . Services are dynamically discovered using Eureka. Backend services process business logic and use caching and databases for performance. Video streaming is handled separately via a CDN, ensuring low latency. DNS | can route to CDN and gateway when hosts is different| otherwise gateway need to resolve CDN vs gateway DNS does not know whether a request is for a CDN or an API by inspecting the request. It simply resolves the requested hostname to the configured destination. For example, cdn.example.com resolves to a CDN, while api.example.com resolves to an API Gateway or Load Balancer. If the same hostname is used for both static content and APIs, the request first reaches the load balancer or reverse proxy, which then routes it based on the URL path or other routing rules.

🌳 🧠 DNS AS A COMPONENT (TREE STYLE) DNS (Domain Name System) ├── Domain Resolution (URL → IP) ├── Hierarchical Lookup ├── Caching (TTL) ├── Geo Routing (CDN use case) └── Load Distribution (basic level)

16CDN & Static/Media Delivery
Understand when the CDN is involved, how cache misses reach origin storage, how the backend returns CDN URLs, and why media is served separately.

CDN | Static/Video Request | backend tells client where to fetch from (CDN URL) Content delivery network (CDN) A CDN is a network of geographically dispersed servers used to deliver static content. CDN servers cache static content like images, videos, CSS, JavaScript files, etc. Here is how CDN works at the high-level: when a user visits a website, a CDN server closest to the user will deliver static content. Intuitively, the further users are from CDN servers, the slower the website loads. For example, if CDN servers are in San Francisco, users in Los Angeles will get content faster than users in Europe. Figure 9 is a great example that shows how CDN improves load time. Request Flow 1. User A tries to get image.png by using an image URL. The URL’s domain is provided by the CDN provider. The following two image URLs are samples used to demonstrate what image URLs look like on Amazon and Akamai CDNs:

https://mysite.cloudfront.net/logo.jpg https://mysite.akamai.com/image-manager/img/logo.jpg 2. If the CDN server does not have image.png in the cache, the CDN server requests the file

from the origin, which can be a web server or online storage like Amazon S3. 3. The origin returns image.png to the CDN server, which includes optional HTTP header Time-to-Live (TTL) which describes how long the image is cached. 4. The CDN caches the image and returns it to User A. The image remains cached in the CDN until the TTL expires. 5. User B sends a request to get the same image. 6. The image is returned from the cache as long as the TTL has not expired. Considerations of using a CDN Cost: CDNs are run by third-party providers, and you are charged for data transfers in and out of the CDN. Caching infrequently used assets provides no significant benefits so you should consider moving them out of the CDN. Setting an appropriate cache expiry: For time-sensitive content, setting a cache expiry time is important. The cache expiry time should neither be too long nor too short. If it is too long, the content might no longer be fresh. If it is too short, it can cause repeat reloading of content from origin servers to the CDN. CDN fallback: You should consider how your website/application copes with CDN failure. If there is a temporary CDN outage, clients should be able to detect the problem and request resources from the origin. Invalidating files: You can remove a file from the CDN before it expires by performing one of the following operations: Invalidate the CDN object using APIs provided by CDN vendors. Use object versioning to serve a different version of the object. To version an object, you can add a parameter to the URL, such as a version number. For example, version number 2 is added to the query string: image.png?v=2. There are TWO TYPES of requests:

1. API Request → goes to Gateway 2. Static/Video Request → goes to CDN CDN (Content Delivery Network) ├── Edge Servers ├── Content Caching ├── Geo Routing ├── Load Distribution └── Origin Fetch

🔹 Case 2: Static / Video Content Client ↓ DNS ↓ CDN ↓ (If not found → Origin Server)
