🧠 1. Partition Tolerance (P) — What actually happens in real
18Distributed Systems Fundamentals
Core distributed-system ideas: partitions, CAP, BASE, scaling, latency, throughput, availability, fault tolerance, hashing, rate limiting, load balancing, caching and backpressure.
Interview-ready

systems What is a Partition? A partition is when two or more servers in a distributed system cannot communicate with each other due to a network failure , even though the servers themselves are still running.

🔥 Problem Scenario You have 2 servers: User → Server A ↔ Server B Now suddenly: Server A ❌ cannot talk to Server B (network failure, but A & B running) 👉 This is called a partition (network split)

💥 What can system do now? Option 1: Stay Available (AP) Both servers keep responding 👉 BUT: Data may be inconsistent 🧠 Example: WhatsApp You send message Other user sees it later System chooses availability over consistency Option 2: Stay Consistent (CP) System blocks requests until sync 👉 BUT: Users may get errors or delays 🧠 Example: Banking Cannot show wrong balance Better to fail than be wrong

🎯 Key Insight 👉 Partition WILL happen in real world So system must choose: Consistency OR Availability
1.6 BASE (Eventual Consistency in Action) 🧠 2. BASE (Eventual Consistency in Action) 🔥 Problem Scenario You upload a post on Instagram 👉 Immediately: You see it ✔ Your friend doesn’t see it ❌ (for few seconds)
💡 Why? Because system is: Basically Available Eventually consistent
🧠 Multiple Scenarios Scenario 1: Social Media Feed You like a post Count updates after few seconds ✔ BASE system Scenario 2: E-commerce Cart Add item → visible immediately Inventory sync later Scenario 3: Distributed DB (Cassandra) Writes go fast

Replication happens later

🎯 Key Insight 👉 BASE = speed first, consistency later

1. Core System Design Fundamentals

1.1 Scalability 🔹 Simple Meaning Scalability = 👉 “Can your system handle more users without breaking?” 🧠 Real-world analogy 10 users → 1 server works 10,000 users → server crashes ❌ 👉 A scalable system = can grow smoothly 🔹 Types of Scaling 1.1.1 Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) 👉 Increase power of one machine More CPU More RAM 💡 Example: t2.micro → t2.large (AWS EC2) ✔ Easy ❌ Limit (you can't scale forever) 1.1.2 Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) 👉 Add more machines Server1 + Server2 + Server3 ✔ Highly scalable ✔ Used in real systems ❌ Needs load balancing 🧠 Interview Insight 👉 Always say:

“We prefer horizontal scaling for large systems”

1.2 Latency vs Throughput 🔹 Latency 👉 Time to serve ONE request Example: Request → Response = 200ms ✔ Lower = better 🔹 Throughput 👉 Number of requests per second Example: 1000 requests/second ✔ Higher = better ⚖ Trade-off Goal Impact Low latency Faster response High throughput Handle more users 🧠 Real-world Example Netflix: Low latency → video starts fast High throughput → millions watching
1.3 Availability vs Consistency 🔹 Availability 👉 System always responds Even if: data is old

partially wrong 🔹 Consistency 👉 Always return latest correct data 🧠 Conflict Example Bank system: Scenario Choice ATM shows balance quickly Availability Exact balance needed Consistency

1.4 CAP Theorem 🔥 Core Idea You can ONLY choose 2 out of 3: Consistency (C) Availability (A) Partition Tolerance (P) 🔹 Partition Tolerance 👉 Network failure between servers 🧠 Real-world systems System Choice Banking CP Netflix AP WhatsApp AP 🎯 Interview Gold Line 👉 “In distributed systems, P is mandatory, so we choose between C and A”
1.5 ACID vs BASE 🔹 ACID (Traditional DB) Atomicity Consistency Isolation Durability ✔ Strong consistency ✔ Used in banking 🔹 BASE (Modern systems) Basically Available Soft state Eventually consistent ✔ Scalable ✔ Used in NoSQL 🧠 Example System Model MySQL ACID Cassandra BASE
1.6 Fault Tolerance 🔹 Meaning 👉 System continues even if something fails 🧠 Example Server crashes → system still works DB fails → backup DB used 🔹 Techniques Replication

Retry Failover

1.7 High Availability 🔹 Meaning 👉 System is almost always UP 🧠 Example 99.99% uptime = ~52 min downtime/year 🔹 Achieved using: Multiple servers Load balancing Failover
1.8 Consistent Hashing 🔹 Problem Adding/removing servers breaks data distribution 🔹 Solution 👉 Consistent hashing distributes data smartly 🧠 Used in: Redis Cassandra 🔥 Key Idea 👉 Only small portion of data moves when scaling
1.9 Rate Limiting 🔹 Why needed? 👉 Protect system from overload / abuse 🔹 Algorithms Token Bucket
Leaky Bucket 🧠 Example User → 100 requests/min allowed
1.10 Load Balancing 🔹 What it does 👉 Distributes traffic across servers 🔹 Types L4 (Transport level) L7 (Application level) 🧠 Algorithms Round Robin Least Connections IP Hash
1.11 Caching Basics 🔹 Why caching? 👉 Avoid hitting DB every time 🧠 Example User Profile → cache → faster response 🔹 Tools Redis Memcached
1.12 Backpressure 🔹 Meaning 👉 System slows down incoming requests when overloaded 🧠 Example Kafka:
consumer slow → producer slowed
🧠 SECTION 1 SUMMARY (Interview Ready) If interviewer asks: 👉 “How do you design scalable system?” You say: - Use horizontal scaling - Add load balancer - Use caching - Apply rate limiting - Ensure fault tolerance - Choose CAP trade-offs
1.9 Consistent Hashing(strategy: circular hash ring) | System

Design -> Distributed System Concepts

System Design │ ├── Distributed System Concepts │ │ ├── CAP Theorem │ │ ├── Consistent Hashing │ │ ├── Eventual Consistency │ │ ├── Rate Limiting │ │ └── Concurrency In normal hashing, adding or removing nodes causes massive data reshuffling, leading to cache

misses and system instability. Consistent hashing minimizes data movement by mapping keys and nodes on a hash ring, ensuring only a small subset of data is affected during scaling. This makes it ideal for distributed systems like caching, databases, and CDNs. “Consistent Hashing is a technique used in distributed systems to distribute keys (like user data or cache entries) across multiple nodes in a way that minimizes the number of keys that need to be moved when nodes are added or removed.

19Consistent Hashing — Deep Dive
Deep dive into why modulo hashing causes large remapping and how a hash ring plus virtual nodes minimizes data movement and hotspots.
Interview-ready

- less keys moved, - map keys and server onto a ring. - =================

🔥 What Problem Consistent Hashing Solves ❌ Problem: Systems break when you scale 🧠 Imagine this real scenario: You built a system: Users → Cache Servers (3 servers) You distribute data like: server = hash(userId) % 3
🚀 Everything works fine… until scaling Now traffic increases → you add 1 more server: server = hash(userId) % 4

💥 What goes wrong? 👉 Almost ALL users go to different servers now Result: Cache becomes useless ❌ Every request hits DB 💥 System slows down badly

🧠 Real-world analogy Imagine: You have 3 grocery stores Customers assigned based on rule Now you open 4th store → 👉 Everyone is reassigned randomly 👉 Chaos 😵
💡 What Consistent Hashing Fixes

✔ Key Idea 👉 When system changes (add/remove server): ONLY small portion of data moves

🧠 Same scenario with Consistent Hashing Before: User A → Server1 User B → Server2 User C → Server3 After adding Server4: Only few users shift to Server4 Rest remain SAME ✔
🎯 Result Problem Without CH With CH Scaling impact Massive ❌ Minimal ✔ Cache loss Almost all ❌ Very little ✔ DB load Spike 💥 Stable ✔
🧠 Why It Is Used (Real Systems Thinking) 🔥 Reason 1: Avoid Cache Collapse Scenario: Redis cache Without consistent hashing: Add node → cache wiped DB overloaded

With consistent hashing: Cache mostly intact ✔

🔥 Reason 2: Smooth Scaling Scenario: Traffic increases Add servers gradually No major data reshuffling 👉 System stays stable
🔥 Reason 3: High Availability Scenario: Server crashes Without CH: Many keys remapped With CH: Only keys of failed server move 👉 Minimal impact
🔥 Reason 4: Efficient Distributed Systems Used in: Redis Cluster Cassandra DynamoDB CDN (Cloudflare)
🧠 Real Production Example 📌 Example: Netflix CDN User requests video Consistent hashing decides which server 👉 If server added/removed: Only small traffic shifts No global disruption
⚡ One-Line Understanding (VERY IMPORTANT) 👉 Consistent hashing is used to:

“Scale distributed systems WITHOUT breaking existing data distribution”

🧠 Interview Answer (Perfect Version) If interviewer asks: 👉 “Why do we use consistent hashing?” You say: In normal hashing, adding or removing nodes causes massive data reshuffling, leading to cache

misses and system instability. Consistent hashing minimizes data movement by mapping keys and nodes on a hash ring, ensuring only a small subset of data is affected during scaling. This makes it ideal for distributed systems like caching, databases, and CDNs.

🚀 Quick Visual Mental Model Normal Hashing: Scaling → Chaos ❌ Consistent Hashing: Scaling → Smooth ✔ ==================================== -Instead of using the typical hash(key) % N strategy, which reassigns nearly all keys when N

changes, consistent hashing maps both keys and servers onto a circular hash ring. -Each key is assigned to the next server in a clockwise direction. -So, when a new server is added, only a small portion of keys (close to that server on the ring) need to be reassigned.

🎯 Add if Asked: “Why not just use modulo hashing?” "The problem with hash(key) % N is that when you change the number of nodes (N), the

mapping of almost all keys changes. That leads to cache misses, performance drops, and a lot of overhead. Consistent hashing avoids this by only remapping keys that fall between two points on the ring, so most of the data remains stable." =============== 🧠 Add if Asked: “How does the ring work?” "We imagine the output of the hash function as a circle (0 to 2³²). Servers and keys are both hashed to positions on this ring. A key is stored in the next server clockwise. For example, if a key hashes to 130° and servers are at 90°, 150°, and 270°, the key goes to the server at 150°. Adding a new server at 140° only affects keys between 130°–140°." ================ 🌟 Bonus: Add if Asked About Load Imbalance "One common improvement is to use virtual nodes, where each physical server is assigned multiple positions on the ring. This helps balance the distribution of keys more evenly and prevents one server from becoming a hotspot."

📌 Keywords to Mention in Your Answer Hash ring Minimal key reassignment Scalability Distributed systems Virtual nodes (if advanced) -->In short, consistent hashing gives us a scalable, fault-tolerant way to distribute data across

servers while avoiding major disruptions when the system topology changes. -->It’s a core design pattern behind systems like DynamoDB, Cassandra, and distributed caching frameworks.” ========================== - Here if some users A,B,C are mapped with servers 1,2,3. Now add new server 4. - So, it might be possible all keys will be reshuffled and all now assigned different server. - So, to avoid such problem, consistent hashing uses Hash ring. ✅ Let's Start With the Core Problem Again You have a distributed cache system with 3 servers (A, B, C). You store keys like this: server = hash(key) % 3 That means:

User hash(key) hash % 3 Server User123 6892 2 C User456 2789 1 B User789 1023 0 A Now, you add a 4th server (D), so your formula becomes: server = hash(key) % 4 The % (modulo) now uses 4 instead of 3 → so ALL keys are re-evaluated. ❗ What happens now? hash("User123") % 4 might be 0 → now goes to Server A hash("User456") % 4 might be 3 → now goes to Server D hash("User789") % 4 might be 1 → now goes to Server B So almost all the user-to-server mappings change! This causes: 💀 Cold cache (servers don't have the right data) 🐢 Slow responses 📉 Inefficient use of cache ⚖ Possible load imbalance 🔍 So… What Problem Does Consistent Hashing Solve? ✅ It avoids reassigning all keys when a new server is added or removed. Instead of % N (where N changes when a server is added), it maps both: Keys (like usernames) Servers (A, B, C, D)...onto a fixed circle (hash ring), and only a small section of keys are affected when servers

change. ======================= 🔄 Okay, So What's the Strategy of Consistent Hashing? Yes! It does follow a specific strategy, and here's how it works: Step-by-Step Strategy: Hash each server to a position on a circle (0 to 2³² — like a clock). Server A = 10° Server B = 120° Server C = 250° Hash each key (username) to a point on the same circle. User123 = 130° Find the next server clockwise from the key’s position. User123 (130°) → next server is Server C (250°) Now if you add a new server (say, Server D at 140°): Only keys between 130° and 140° move to D. All other key assignments stay the same! 🎉 ✅ This solves the exact remapping problem we saw with hash(key) % N. ===============

🔥 1. The REAL Problem (Why we need it) Scenario: Normal Hashing (BAD) You have 3 cache servers: Server1, Server2, Server3 You distribute users like: server = hash(userId) % 3

💥 Now scaling happens 👉 You add a new server: Server4 added Now: server = hash(userId) % 4 ❌ Disaster 👉 Almost ALL users get remapped Cache miss everywhere DB overloaded 💥 System slowdown

🧠 Real-world impact Redis cluster suddenly useless CDN cache wiped

Huge latency spike

💡 2. Solution: Consistent Hashing 👉 Idea: Don’t use % (modulo) Instead use a circular ring
🔵 3. Hash Ring Concept Step 1: Imagine a circle 0 → 360 degrees (or 0 → MAX_HASH)
Step 2: Place servers on ring hash(Server1) → position on ring hash(Server2) → position hash(Server3) → position
Step 3: Place keys (users) hash(userId) → position on ring

Step 4: Assignment rule 👉 Move clockwise until you find a server

🧠 Example (user) → → → Server2
🔥 4. What happens when adding a server? Add Server4 👉 Only nearby keys move Only small portion of data shifts

✅ Result Before After 100% data moved ❌ ~25% moved ✔

🧠 Key Insight 👉 Consistent hashing = “Minimal data movement during scaling”
⚠ 5. Problem in Consistent Hashing (Hotspots) Scenario What if servers are unevenly placed? Server1 → large range Server2 → small range 👉 Server1 overloaded 💥
💡 6. Solution: Virtual Nodes (VERY IMPORTANT) Idea 👉 Each server gets multiple positions on ring Server1 → S1a, S1b, S1c Server2 → S2a, S2b, S2c

✅ Result Load evenly distributed No hotspots
